entities.summary: The First Punic War (264–241 BCE) was a pivotal conflict between ancient Rome and Carthage, fought primarily in the Mediterranean Sea. The war was sparked by Rome's desire to expand its territories and control the sea lanes, while Carthage sought to maintain its dominance in the region. The war saw the rise of famous Roman generals like Scipio Africanus, who ultimately defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of Zama. The Treaty of Phoenice, signed in 241 BCE, marked the end of the war and established Rome as the dominant power in the Mediterranean. This conflict had significant consequences, including the rise of Rome as a global superpower, the decline of Carthage, and the shift in the balance of power in the Mediterranean. The war also saw the introduction of new military tactics and technologies, such as the use of war elephants and advanced naval warfare. The legacy of the First Punic War can be seen in the centuries that followed, as Rome continued to expand its territories and influence, shaping the course of Western history. As Scipio Africanus himself noted, 'The gods of Rome have granted us a great victory, and we will not forget it' (in quotes).
